## How to use this

The code from Lecture 18, filled in, with the numbers it produces.

. . .

Optimizers are numerical, so your last decimal place may differ from mine. Any
`NaNs produced` warnings while fitting are harmless here: the optimizer tried an
impossible value on its way to the answer.

::: {.notes}
Posted after class so nobody is left wondering whether their answer was right.
:::

## Setting up {.smaller}

```{r}
library(bbmle)

occ <- read.csv("https://github.com/bmaitner/biometry_course/raw/refs/heads/main/data/class_examples/bobwhite_occupancy.csv")
counts <- read.csv("https://github.com/bmaitner/biometry_course/raw/refs/heads/main/data/class_examples/bobwhite_counts.csv")

occ_nll2 <- function(params, n_occupied, n_routes, elapsed){
  p <- plogis(params[1] + params[2] * elapsed)
  -sum(dbinom(n_occupied, size = n_routes, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}
parnames(occ_nll2) <- c("a", "b")
occ_data <- list(n_occupied = occ$n_occupied, n_routes = occ$n_routes,
                 elapsed = occ$elapsed)
m_occ <- mle2(minuslogl = occ_nll2, start = c(a = 2, b = -0.05), data = occ_data)
m_occ@min
```

With `library(biometrydata)` installed, `occ <- bobwhite_occupancy` and
`counts <- bobwhite_counts` give the same tables.

## A nonsense predictor {.smaller}

```{r}
set.seed(1)                   # yours had no seed, so your number differs
junk <- runif(nrow(occ))

occ_junk <- function(params, n_occupied, n_routes, elapsed, junk){
  p <- plogis(params[1] + params[2] * elapsed + params[3] * junk)
  -sum(dbinom(n_occupied, size = n_routes, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}
parnames(occ_junk) <- c("a", "b", "c")

m_junk <- mle2(minuslogl = occ_junk, start = c(a = 2, b = -0.05, c = 0),
               data = c(occ_data, list(junk = junk)))

m_occ@min - m_junk@min
anova(m_occ, m_junk)
```

Positive, as it must be, and small. The test does not come close to supporting it.

## The likelihood ratio test {.smaller}

```{r}
const_nll <- function(params, n_occupied, n_routes){
  p <- plogis(params[1])
  -sum(dbinom(n_occupied, size = n_routes, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}
parnames(const_nll) <- "a"
m_const <- mle2(minuslogl = const_nll, start = c(a = 1),
                data = list(n_occupied = occ$n_occupied, n_routes = occ$n_routes))

deviance_occ <- 2 * (m_const@min - m_occ@min)
deviance_occ
pchisq(deviance_occ, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

## Three models, and AIC by hand {.smaller}

```{r}
m_flat <- mle2(count ~ dnbinom(mu = mu0, size = k),
               start = list(mu0 = 10, k = 1.4), data = counts)

m_year <- mle2(count ~ dnbinom(mu = mu0 * exp(r * elapsed), size = k),
               start = list(mu0 = 15, r = -0.03, k = 1.4), data = counts)

m_urban <- mle2(count ~ dnbinom(mu = mu0 * exp(b * frac_built), size = k),
                start = list(mu0 = 12, b = -3, k = 1.4), data = counts)

AIC(m_flat)
2 * m_flat@min + 2 * 2
```

## Year and development {.smaller}

```{r}
m_both <- mle2(count ~ dnbinom(mu = mu0 * exp(b * frac_built + r * elapsed),
                               size = k),
               start = list(mu0 = 15, b = -3, r = -0.03, k = 1.4),
               data = counts)

AICtab(m_flat, m_year, m_urban, m_both, base = TRUE)
```

. . .

`m_both` is best by a wide margin. Year against development is **not** a nested
pair, so only AIC can rank those two; development alone beats year alone by about
43 units.

## The two species {.smaller}

```{r}
birds <- read.csv("https://github.com/bmaitner/biometry_course/raw/refs/heads/main/data/class_examples/bbs_two_species.csv")
birds$species <- factor(birds$species, levels = c("cardinal", "bobwhite"))

form <- count ~ dnbinom(mu = exp(log_mu0 + b * frac_built), size = exp(log_k))
start <- list(log_mu0 = 2, b = 0, log_k = 0)

m_same <- mle2(form, start = start, data = birds)
m_mu   <- mle2(form, start = start, data = birds, parameters = list(log_mu0 ~ species))
m_b    <- mle2(form, start = start, data = birds, parameters = list(b ~ species))
m_mub  <- mle2(form, start = start, data = birds,
               parameters = list(log_mu0 ~ species, b ~ species))
m_muk  <- mle2(form, start = start, data = birds,
               parameters = list(log_mu0 ~ species, log_k ~ species))
m_all  <- mle2(form, start = start, data = birds,
               parameters = list(log_mu0 ~ species, b ~ species, log_k ~ species))
```

With the package installed, `birds <- bbs_two_species` gives the same table.

## Comparing them {.smaller}

```{r}
AICtab(m_same, m_mu, m_b, m_mub, m_muk, m_all, base = TRUE, weights = TRUE)
```

. . .

`m_all` is best: the species differ in all three ways.

## Back-transforming `m_all` {.smaller}

```{r}
cf <- coef(m_all)

exp(cf["log_mu0.(Intercept)"])                               # cardinals, nothing built
exp(cf["log_mu0.(Intercept)"] + cf["log_mu0.speciesbobwhite"]) # bobwhite, nothing built

log(2) / abs(cf["b.(Intercept)"])                            # cardinals halve every...
log(2) / abs(cf["b.(Intercept)"] + cf["b.speciesbobwhite"])  # bobwhite halve every...
```

Cardinals: about 54 birds where nothing is built, halving with every 37% of
development. Bobwhite: about 8, halving with every 9%. Bobwhite also have the
smaller `k`, so they are patchier from route to route.

## Additional practice: does the development effect change over time? {.smaller}

```{r}
m_int <- mle2(count ~ dnbinom(mu = mu0 * exp(b * frac_built + r * elapsed +
                                           i * frac_built * elapsed),
                              size = k),
              start = list(mu0 = 15, b = -3, r = -0.03, i = 0, k = 1.4),
              data = counts)

anova(m_both, m_int)
AICtab(m_both, m_int, base = TRUE)
```

## What the practice shows {.smaller}

`m_both` is nested in `m_int`: set `i = 0`. So both tools apply.

. . .

The test: $p$ = 0.14, not supported. AIC: a difference of 0.2, a tie.

. . .

They do not really disagree. A difference under 2 means the data cannot tell the
models apart, and with a tie the **simpler model** is the one to report. So:
development matters, year matters, and there is no evidence that the effect of
development has changed over the 23 years.
